The card takes their mean, 1.0, and their standard deviation, q = 0.29; a perfectly layered web would score 0." width="100%"} The trophic incoherence parameter `q` (Johnson et al., 2014) is the standard deviation of the trophic differences over all edges (see `trophic_differences()`). A perfectly layered network, where every edge climbs exactly one level, has `q = 0`; higher values mean edges skip levels or loop back. Trophic coherence predicts stability in food webs and appears in gene regulation, neural and other directed networks: coherent networks tend to have few cycles and to be more stable. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether trophic levels weight diets by edge weight. If `None` (default), follows the graph. [cannibalism]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `False` (default), self-loops are removed before computing levels and differences, as in NetworkX. If `True`, they are kept. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The trophic incoherence parameter `q` (population standard deviation). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : As for `trophic_levels()`. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~trophic_levels`) : The node levels. [](`~trophic_differences`) : The level difference across each edge. [](`~global_reaching_centrality`) : Another single-number test of hierarchy. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A food chain is perfectly coherent. Adding an omnivore link that skips a level makes it less so: ::: {#1cd79417 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec chain = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("plant", "herbivore"), ("herbivore", "carnivore")], directed=True ) coherent = chain.trophic_incoherence_parameter() chain.add_edge("plant", "carnivore") coherent, chain.trophic_incoherence_parameter() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.0, 0.408248290463863) ``` ::: ::: ### Prerequisites and citations The prerequisites in `courses()` mostly climb one level at a time, so `q` is fairly low. Citations are far less orderly: a paper can cite last year's work and a classic from twenty years before. Here `citations()` is reversed, so that its edges point from a paper to the later papers that build on it: ::: {#ff48bf59 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} cited = ec.citations().reverse() ( ec.courses().trophic_incoherence_parameter(), cited.trophic_incoherence_parameter(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (0.36674640281345394, 0.7885924015747676) ``` ::: ::: Drawn with each citation as wide as its trophic difference, the widest edges run from the two oldest papers straight to recent ones: ::: {#281c4476 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} cited = cited.set_edge_attrs("difference", cited.trophic_differences()) cited.plot( layout="pos", color_by="field", label_by="label", edge_width_by="difference", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
